title: Checkpoint: Modern Masters
objective: After this level you can compare the great modern architects and their ideas.
summary: The Pritzker Prize (1979) honors a living architect's built work. Modern masters found form in nature, in the machine and in new geometry.

cards.headline: Modern Masters finale: architecture has its own Nobel. Three of ours won it.
cards.body: Frank Gehry won the Pritzker Prize in 1989, Jørn Utzon in 2003 and Zaha Hadid in 2004, the first woman to win. What does the prize reward? And how do this chapter's ideas fit together?

cards.headline: The Pritzker Prize
cards.body: The Pritzker family of Chicago set up the prize in 1979, through their Hyatt Foundation. Each year it honors a living architect whose built work shows talent, vision and commitment. It's often called architecture's Nobel, and many of its procedures are modeled on the Nobel Prize. The winner receives $100,000 and a bronze medallion. Note the word built: Hadid, the former paper architect, won for buildings that stood.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: Where modern masters found their forms: in nature, in the machine and in new geometry.
How a frame freed the walls, from Le Corbusier's five points to Mies's glass and 'less is more'.
Why Gaudí designed with upside-down hanging models and let his columns lean like trees.
What Brutalism really means, and why people still argue over buildings like it.

questions.prompt: Whom does the Pritzker Architecture Prize honor each year?

options.label: A living architect, for built work
The best unbuilt competition design
An architect from any era, living or dead
The tallest building finished that year
options.rationale: It honors an architect, not a building.

questions.explanation: Each year the Pritzker Prize honors a living architect whose built work shows talent, vision and commitment.

questions.prompt: Modern Masters recap: which two architects took their forms from nature?

options.label: Le Corbusier and Mies
options.rationale: They looked to the machine and simplicity.

options.label: Utzon and Gehry
Gaudí and Wright
Gropius and Breuer
options.rationale: The Bauhaus aimed at the factory.

questions.explanation: Gaudí's columns stand like trees, and Wright's Fallingwater echoes the rock ledges around it.

questions.prompt: On the Modern Masters timeline, what came between the founding of the Bauhaus and the finishing of Fallingwater?

options.label: Gaudí takes over the Sagrada Família
Mies's Barcelona Pavilion
The Sydney Opera House is completed
The Guggenheim Bilbao opens

questions.explanation: The Bauhaus was founded in 1919, the Barcelona Pavilion was built for 1929, and Fallingwater was finished in 1937.

questions.prompt: Modern Masters recap: what did critic Witold Rybczynski argue about eye-catching museum buildings?

options.label: They always pay for themselves
They should all be clad in titanium
They must be designed with CATIA
They don't reliably bring the crowds

questions.explanation: In 2011 Rybczynski argued that eye-catching museum architecture doesn't by itself bring crowds, calling Bilbao an anomaly.

questions.prompt: Modern Masters recap: what inspired Marcel Breuer's 1925 tubular steel chair?

options.label: The frame of a railway carriage
Scaffolding at the Bauhaus site
The handlebars of his bicycle
A chair in the Barcelona Pavilion
options.rationale: Breuer's chair came first, from a bicycle.

questions.explanation: Breuer's tubular steel club chair was inspired by the handlebars of his bicycle.
